text:
Recent work supports separating persistent preferences from immediate intent, then learning their mixture. HeteroTempRec (2026) combines local convolutional features, global attention, and personalized temporal fusion; LSTASRec (2025 preprint) combines long-history attention, a short-term LSTM/local-attention branch, and adaptive gating. These suggest a practical SASRec extension: retain its causal encoder, add a cheap recent-window representation and pooled historical preference, and learn a gate from observed sequence features. Reported results do not establish gains on this pinned benchmark. [HeteroTempRec](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ins.2025.122703), [LSTASRec](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5238143).

Elapsed time can govern both attention and fusion. TLSRec explicitly uses time lag to regulate long- versus short-term contributions; HyTRec (2026 preprint) separates stable preferences from intent spikes and upweights fresh behavior. A lightweight experiment could use bucketed log-time gaps as attention biases and gate inputs, with causal masking throughout. At inference, use only timestamps available in the supplied history; an unknown next-interaction timestamp cannot supply a query-time feature. [TLSRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.04760), [HyTRec](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.18283).

Amazon’s repeat-purchase research models item replenishment probability and purchase timing, but that objective differs from unseen-item recommendation. It does not justify blanket suppression of recently encountered durable goods or treating interactions as confirmed purchases. Here, “recently satisfied need” remains a hypothesis: test learned recency effects against SASRec using macro validation HR@10, with separate ablations for the extra preference branch, gate, and temporal features. [Buy It Again](https://assets.amazon.science/40/e5/89556a6341eaa3d7dacc074ff24d/buy-it-again-modeling-repeat-purchase-recommendations.pdf).
